       1             SENATOR BONACIC:  First of all, good morning.

       2             Today is April 30, 2013.

       3             I'm Senator Bonacic.  I chair the Senate

       4      Judiciary Committee meeting.

       5             The business of the day will be, this now

       6      will be a public hearing, to hear from witnesses on

       7      the Governor's nominee to the Court of Appeals.

       8             The -- I would like to acknowledge my ranking

       9      member, Senator John Sampson.

      10             Today we're going to have two witnesses that

      11      will provide oral testimony about

      12      Judge Abdus-Salaam's qualifications.

      13             The witnesses will be:

      14             Professor Michael Hutter, who is an Albany

      15      Law School professor, and a practicing attorney;

      16             And also, Michael Jaffe, who's president of

      17      the New York State Trial Lawyers Association.

      18             We're going to ask each witness to limit

      19      their testimony to ten minutes.

      20             On Thursday, April 25th, I had issued a

      21      Judiciary report to our members.

      22             I think the Governor has nominated a very

      23      experienced, well-rounded judicial nominee for our

      24      highest bench.

      25             As you will hear today, in her career, she





 

                                                                   5
       1      is, both, a practicing attorney, and she has served

       2      as judge of the Supreme Court, and an appellate

       3      [unintelligible] judge for the First Department.

       4             She has engaged in legal analysis on areas

       5      of law, including, but not limited, to

       6      corporations, contracts, criminal, real estate,

       7      personal injury, landlord-tenant,

       8      estate surrogates, banking, civil rights, health,

       9      labor, evidence.

      10             And, in reviewing her background, I think

      11      she's made rulings on 211 cases.

      12             So, I would now like to invite

      13      Senator Sampson to address the Committee.

      14             SENATOR SAMPSON:  Thank you very much,

      15      Chairman Bonacic, and to my colleagues, and also to

      16      our -- everyone who's attending.

      17             The only thing I can say is, this judge has

      18      impeccable credentials, impeccable qualifications,

      19      impeccable experience, and this judge is what I call

      20      "a complete jurist."

      21             And I look forward to hearing from those, but

      22      also look forward to hearing from her, in this

      23      public-hearing process, and, look forward to the

      24      questions from my colleagues, because I think,

      25      without question, this is one of the best





 

                                                                   6
       1      selections the Governor has made to the Court of

       2      Appeals.

       3             So, thank you very much, Chairman.

       4             SENATOR BONACIC:  Thank you, Senator Sampson.

       5             I would ask Mr. Hutter to please come up.

       6             And while he's coming up, I would like to

       7      acknowledge the members of the Judiciary Committee

       8      that are here:

       9             Senator Perkins, Senator O'Mara,

      10      Senator LaValle, Senator Breslin, Senator Lanza,

      11      Senator Fuschillo, Senator Savino,

      12      Senator DeFrancisco, Senator Nozzolio,

      13      Senator Sampson, Senator Hoylman, Senator Little,

      14      Senator Flanagan, Senator Ruth Hassell-Thompson,

      15      Senator Dilan, Senator Espaillat, and last, but not

      16      least, Senator Toby Stavisky.

      17             SENATOR STAVISKY:  Just because I'm not a

      18      lawyer, you don't have to put me as "last."

      19                  [Laughter.]

      20             SENATOR BONACIC:  Mr. Hutter, first of all,

      21      good morning.

      22             MICHAEL HUTTER:  Good morning, sir,

      23      Mr. Chairman.

      24             SENATOR BONACIC:  Thank you for being here.

      25             Please tell us a little bit about, who you





 

                                                                   7
       1      are, your background, and your experience, and, how

       2      do you know this nominee.

       3             MICHAEL HUTTER:  I'm presently a professor of

       4      law at the Albany Law School.  I've been there since

       5      1976.

       6             I also maintain a private practice,

       7      specializing in appeals.  I've been doing that now

       8      for over 40 years.

       9             My background, with respect to getting into

      10      appellate work, is I, as a law clerk for

      11      Judge Matthew Jasen, the Court of Appeals,

      12      1970 to 1972.

      13             And, I've argued over 35 cases before the

      14      court, not only representing clients, but also

      15      submitting amicus briefs on various issues

      16      involving state government, legislative

      17      prerogatives, and the like.

      18             I have also -- and this is my way of

      19      introduction to Judge Abdus-Salaam's judging, is I

      20      also provide updates for the judges on civil

      21      evidence, criminal-law matters, various topics,

      22      that the judges need to know, on an annual basis,

      23      at the judges' school, and also through the

      24      Judicial Institute.

      25             And through that, I became aware of





 

                                                                   8
       1      Judge Abdus-Salaam's writings.

       2             And prior to her even being nominated, I was

       3      commenting very favorably on her abilities as a

       4      judge, and her demonstrated excellence in her

       5      opinion writing.

       6             And it's on the basis of that, that I would

       7      offer my testimony today, Senator.

       8             SENATOR BONACIC:  Okay, thank you,

       9      Mr. Hutter.

      10             You yourself have been practicing law, how

      11      long?

      12             MICHAEL HUTTER:  Pardon me?

      13             SENATOR BONACIC:  How long you have been

      14      practicing law?

      15             MICHAEL HUTTER:  Since 1972, after the end of

      16      my clerkship.

      17             SENATOR BONACIC:  So you wear two hats:

      18      You're a professor, and you get out in the trenches

      19      and you practice law?

      20             MICHAEL HUTTER:  Yes.  And I've argued in

      21      that respect, about 35 cases in the Court of

      22      Appeals.

      23             Overall, about 350 appeals since 1972 in

      24      all of New York's appellate courts.

      25             SENATOR BONACIC:  Okay.





 

                                                                   9
       1             All right, does anyone have any questions of

       2      Mr. Hutter?

       3             Senator Sampson.

       4             SENATOR SAMPSON:  Professor Hutter, I just

       5      want to thank you for my "A" in Evidence you gave me

       6      when I was in law school.

       7                  [Laughter.]

       8             MICHAEL HUTTER:  It was well deserved,

       9      Senator.

      10                  [Laughter.]

      11             MICHAEL HUTTER:  I was going to -- after I

      12      had a chance, I was going to acknowledge your

      13      presence here as a former student.

      14             I'm very honored to be here with you.

      15             SENATOR BONACIC:  Do you have some remarks

      16      that you would like to make?

      17             MICHAEL HUTTER:  Ah, yes, if I may, a couple

      18      of things.

      19             I think both Senators Sampson and Bonacic

      20      have talked about the basic background.

      21             Let me make a couple of comments about her

      22      judging, and I'll reference a couple of cases that

      23      she talked about.

      24             In looking at it, I think there are five

      25      major characteristics of her decisions, on a





 

                                                                   10
       1      consistent basis, whether it is dissenting or in the

       2      majority.

       3             First, it is a very accurate characterization

       4      of the facts, in the sense that, she goes through

       5      the brief, she goes through the records, isolates

       6      what's important, and then ignores what's really

       7      ridiculous.

       8             I can say that because, in commenting and

       9      writing on her decisions, to get into the full

      10      flavor, I have looked at the briefs, and I've seen

      11      no situations where she's mischaracterizing facts.

      12             So, she's putting cases in a proper context.

      13             Secondly, it is clearly a fidelity to the

      14      law.

      15             In that respect, clearly, there's no tortured

      16      reasoning, or trying to pick apart precedent that

      17      she may not like, or it may be interfering with a

      18      possible goal.

      19             There's none of that.

      20             I think, also, it's very important for this

      21      body to realize as well, is that, in interpreting

      22      statutes, she is very faithful to legislative

      23      history, and legislative intent.

      24             Consistently, she's looking at, "What did the

      25      Legislature intend?" and trying to effectuate that.





 

                                                                   11
       1             There's no instances where she tried to

       2      frustrate a legislative goal because she may

       3      disagree with it.  There's no indication of that

       4      whatsoever.

       5             She really, again, has had fidelity to the

       6      law.

       7             Third, in that regard, stare decisis, she's

       8      using as a guide, but she's not bound by it, in the

       9      sense that it's something that can be, you must

      10      always adhere it to.

      11             Now, stare decisis, clearly, is a very

      12      important doctrine, where we recognize precedent.

      13      We just don't simply change because we are changing

      14      views, but it's a guide to certainty, to make sure

      15      that we have legitimacy; that we're not just making

      16      ad hoc decisions.

      17             But the way she uses it, and I'll point out

      18      two cases in a minute, certainty is certainly a

      19      means to an end, but it's not an end of itself.

      20             And the end itself, of course, is justice.

      21             And I think, in that respect, where she has

      22      seen a bad decision from her own court several

      23      years earlier, or 20 years earlier, she's ready

      24      now to -- now if -- "We can't follow it anymore, and

      25      here are the reasons why."





 

                                                                   12
       1             And that leads to the fourth the thing:

       2      There's an exceptional clarity and thoroughness to

       3      her writings.

       4             In that respect, it's not simply a plaintiff

       5      wins, or, I disagree, or, this case is binding;

       6      rather, you see her consistently, breaking down,

       7      taking the arguments as raised in the brief, and

       8      going through them, and then rejecting them or

       9      accepting them.

      10             There's no ipse dixit statements.  It's

      11      consistent.  The thoroughness is amazing.

      12             And it's something that I learned from

      13      Matt Jasen, when I clerked with him, is the ideas,

      14      that you're writing a decision for the bar and the

      15      bench, and you want to provide guidance.  Make

      16      yourself clear, and make sure that everyone knows

      17      what the holding is.

      18             I mean, when you read a Judge Abdus-Salaam

      19      decision, you know what holding is.

      20             And in that regard, she's hitting the issue

      21      that's raised.  There's no hidden agenda in trying

      22      to suggest alternatives or future issues.  She's

      23      right on the money.

      24             And then, lastly, I think here, in doing

      25      that, she's also, where, clearly, the consequences





 

                                                                   13
       1      of decisions, in the sense that, she'll look at it:

       2             If I go this way, as defendant is arguing, or

       3      plaintiff is arguing, that, here are the problems.

       4      But, we don't have those problems that way.

       5             And she shows, really, and I think this is

       6      the basis of her substantial record of achievement

       7      at the bar, and then on the appellate court, and the

       8      trial court, she's aware of the practical

       9      consequences of her decision, and she's ever mindful

      10      of that.

      11             I think, here, she's got a terrific

      12      background that serves her well as a judge in

      13      getting across these views.

      14             Now -- and I say "these views," again, the

      15      view, only thing that I could see is fidelity to the

      16      law.  I saw no indication that she has a distinctive

      17      philosophy: this is what she wants to achieve, or

      18      anything like that.

      19             She's following what the Legislature wants,

      20      and she's following what the courts want.

      21             And I think in that respect, clearly, the

      22      idea of legitimacy with courts, is that's what you

      23      want with judges.

      24             I think, here, there's a sense then, when you

      25      appear before Judge Abdus-Salaam, you got a fair





 

                                                                   14
       1      shake.  You have the law given to you.  You have the

       2      arguments thrown out, analyzed, and thoroughly

       3      discussed.

       4             And I think, here, if I were on a losing

       5      side, I know -- I think I'd say:  You know what?  I

       6      should have lost.

       7             I mean, that's how thorough her analysis is.

       8             And I think it's interesting in that respect,

       9      when you look at a couple of her decisions.

      10             And the one decision I'll mention, this is

      11      the Beach [ph.] case, with respect to:  What happens

      12      when a lawyer, in preparing a witness, gives that

      13      witness -- for a deposition, gives that witness

      14      privileged documents?

      15             Now, the law in that regard had been kind of

      16      cloudy.  There was a very distinct First Department

      17      decision that was creating a lot of problems.

      18             She went right into it, and she said:  Here's

      19      what the problem is.

      20             And she corrected it; she said:  We're not

      21      going to follow that decision, and this is why.

      22             And in doing so, she laid forth some very

      23      clear rulings regarding the use of privileged

      24      documents, with respect to prepping witnesses,

      25      which is extremely important for the practicing bar.





 

                                                                   15
       1             Now, there's a temptation that maybe she

       2      should have talked about what will happen at trial

       3      if you give a witness.  But, that wasn't the issue.

       4             And she simply limited herself to what the

       5      issue is.  No suggestions here, or dropping

       6      hints, and maybe a different result later on.

       7             She's right on the money.

       8             A second case that has been favorably

       9      discussed on the bar, is her decision in

      10      Martin versus Portech, the use of electronic

      11      signatures to sign an affirmation by a physician,

      12      under CPLR 2306.

      13             CPLR 20306 [sic], of course, allows lawyers,

      14      physicians, osteopaths, dentists, podiatrists, to

      15      provide affirmations in lieu of an affidavit.

      16             Well, this legislature, it passed the state

      17      technology law, Section 304, which said:  Electronic

      18      signatures will have the full force of a written

      19      signature.

      20             And the question now is:  Does that now apply

      21      equally to affirmations?

      22             It would apply to contracts, it would apply

      23      to other writings; but what about affirmations?

      24             Is there anything magic?

      25             The Second Department had said:  Well, it's





 

                                                                   16
       1      different.  There's got to be -- affirmations are

       2      not good.

       3             And so what Judge Abdus-Salaam looked at,

       4      well, she looked at 2306 of the CPLR.  It made no

       5      exception for affirmations with respect to

       6      electronic signatures.  Nothing there.

       7             It just said, "writings."

       8             And then she looked at the language of 304;

       9      the legislative intent was to allow, in all

      10      instances, electronic signatures to be a full

      11      substitute for signatures, why not?

      12             Now, interestingly, there's some discussion

      13      regarding, well, she may have not clarified.

      14             What about affidavits?  How do you do

      15      electronic signatures with an affidavit where you

      16      have the notary?

      17             And that's an interesting issue, but it was

      18      not presented.

      19             And, so, to somehow criticize her for maybe

      20      not getting into an area that was not addressed by

      21      the brief, is really absurd.

      22             I mean, she limited herself to a clear

      23      decision, pointed out.  She respectfully dissented

      24      from the view of the Second Department.  Gave it,

      25      certainly, the respect that it's due, and then





 

                                                                   17
       1      pointed out its shortcomings.

       2             And not just simply, I disagree, but here are

       3      the reasons why I disagree.

       4             So in that respect, if I'm a

       5      Second Department judge, I think I'd look at this,

       6      and say:  You know what?  Maybe we did get it wrong.

       7             Now, hopefully, that case will go up one

       8      point, to the Court of Appeals, but we just don't

       9      know.

      10             The other thing is that, with her dissents,

      11      and I picked out two dissents of recent value

      12      here, that I think to this Committee:

      13             In the matter of New York County Lawyers

      14      versus Bloomberg, issue came up with respect to the

      15      adequacy of the assigned counsel plan in New York

      16      City:

      17             When there's a conflict among the primary

      18      legal-aid bureau, who is going to then provide

      19      counsel when there's a conflict, and legal aid was

      20      already representing one of the defendants in the

      21      matter, or a witness?

      22             And the City of New York had changed its

      23      rules, and now allowed, kind of, private legal-aid

      24      bureaus, instead of going with

      25      county-representation plans, and other things.





 

                                                                   18
       1             The judge, Jim Yates, the present counsel

       2      to Assemblyman Silver, wrote a very good decision, a

       3      Supreme Court, very thoughtful.

       4             The majority of the Appellate Division

       5      basically agreed with that.

       6             Again, in a very thoughtful decision,

       7      Judge Abdus-Salaam dissented.

       8             And when you read her dissent, what she did

       9      is, she went through all of the assigned counsel

      10      plans, pointed out the -- what they were trying to

      11      do, and then went to the Legislature with Section, I

      12      think, 722 of the County law, indicating, this is

      13      what the Legislature wanted.

      14             And she disagreed with the majority,

      15      disagreed with Judge Yates, and pointed out:  This

      16      is clear in the Legislature.

      17             Now, the Court of Appeals disagreed, the

      18      majority, but she drew an interesting combination of

      19      people who agree with her view:

      20             Chief Judge Lippman, Judge Pickett, and

      21      Judge Smith.

      22             I don't think that we've ever seen those

      23      three agree on a dissenting opinion together, but I

      24      think that's the type of thought that she will

      25      develop.





 

                                                                   19
       1             Lastly, I mentioned here, there's another

       2      decision of hers that just came down recently, the

       3      first -- the Court of Appeals.  This is the Lewis

       4      decision; an interesting decision with respect to a

       5      personal-injury action, in the context of a false

       6      arrest.

       7             A person is accused now of stealing laptops

       8      and selling them.  A jury verdict in favor of the

       9      plaintiff, finding there was no probable cause for

      10      the City -- New York City police to make the arrest.

      11             She dissented, and, along with

      12      Judge Friedman.

      13             And you can see, I think, a lot of her work

      14      in it.

      15             Although she was not the author of the

      16      decision, based upon other things in her background,

      17      it's clear that she worked on this decision closely

      18      with Judge Friedman, and pointed out some of the

      19      problems with probable cause in the neighborhood,

      20      indicating, that, Hey, I think, here, the police did

      21      have probable cause, based upon all this.

      22             A very sensible approach of the evidence.

      23             And, low and behold, the Court of Appeals,

      24      just two months ago, reversed, on the basis of

      25      that dissenting opinion.





 

                                                                   20
       1             So in that respect, again, I think, here,

       2      when you grab hold of a Judge Abdus-Salaam decision,

       3      it is a very thoughtful one.

       4             I think, certainly, if I'm a lawyer going up

       5      to a higher court, or any court, and I have an

       6      Abdus-Salaam decision, to follow, I would -- I would

       7      be very happy.

       8             And if I could add one last thing:

       9             I think, here, as well, and I told this story

      10      to Senator Bonacic, and, I mentioned it to

      11      Judge Abdus-Salaam, and she laughed a little bit:

      12             Last summer, I had the privilege of

      13      addressing the Association of Supreme Court

      14      Judges' Conference in Saratoga, talking about

      15      recent decisions.

      16             And, the association is a raucous crowd.

      17      They're very opinionated, and they have their own

      18      views.

      19             You put 100 of those judges in one room,

      20      you'll get 110 opinions.  They all have their own

      21      different views on it.

      22             And I talked about this recent decision, the

      23      Beach decision, and I said:  This is a very

      24      thoughtful decision by Judge Abdus-Salaam.  You've

      25      got to follow it; she laid it out, and, it should be





 

                                                                   21
       1      very clear, and in a very important area.

       2             Now, I have a reputation, in talking at

       3      these, I'm very candid.

       4             If a decision stinks, I'll say it.

       5             If a decision is wrong, or there are

       6      problems, I'll say it.

       7             So a voice in the back shouts out, "What do

       8      you really think of it?"

       9             And I said:  This is a setup.  What's going

      10      on?

      11             And I said:  Well, what I really think, it's

      12      a terrific decision.

      13             And all of a sudden, there was full applause.

      14      Everyone was applauding.

      15             And then I found out later,

      16      Judge Abdus-Salaam was in the audience.

      17                  [Laughter.]

      18             MICHAEL HUTTER:  And I thought that

      19      indicates, clearly, that she has the respect of

      20      her peers.

      21             So I think, here, that the Governor has made

      22      an excellent choice.

      23             This Committee, obviously, has the right now

      24      to look into that.  You have that responsibility.

      25             By discussions with your staff, it's clear





 

                                                                   22
       1      that you're taking this responsibility very

       2      seriously; not just accepting empty assurances of

       3      this candidate as the best thing since sliced bread,

       4      or whatever, but looking at the record.

       5             And I would clearly support this nomination.

       6             I think when you look at the record, you have

       7      a person of substantial achievement at the bar,

       8      substantial achievement as a judge.

       9             And I think the only limitation that would be

      10      here, is we're only going to have her, maybe, for

      11      ten years.

      12             I'd like to have her for a lot longer than

      13      that on this court.

      14             I think she's a superb choice.

      15             I think the Governor should be applauded for

      16      this choice.

      17             And, I would urge this Committee to look at

      18      this very favorably: her candidacy.

      19             SENATOR BONACIC:  Thank you, Professor.

      20             Anybody have any questions of

      21      Professor Hutter?

      22             Well, I was very impressed with the depth of

      23      your analysis.

      24             I thank you for taking the time, and sharing

      25      your views with us.  It's very insightful.





 

                                                                   23
       1             Thank you.

       2             MICHAEL HUTTER:  Thank you for the

       3      opportunity, Senator.

       4             SENATOR BONACIC:  Okay.  Our next, and final

       5      witness, is Michael Jaffe, president of the New York

       6      State Trial Lawyers Association.

       7             Michael?

       8             MICHAEL JAFFE:  Good morning, Senator.

       9             SENATOR BONACIC:  Michael, I think you have

      10      some prepared remarks you'd like to share with us on

      11      behalf of the New York State Trial Lawyers

      12      Association?

      13             MICHAEL JAFFE:  Yes, Senator.  Thank you.

      14             And I would start off by saying:  Thank you,

      15      Chairman Bonacic, and thank you to the Committee,

      16      for having us here this morning.

      17             I must agree with everything that

      18      Professor Hutter said, and he said it, well, better

      19      than I could possible state it.

      20             I think the choice of Justice Abdus-Salaam

      21      for the Court of Appeals is a wonderful decision

      22      and wonderful choice that the Governor has made.

      23             I am the president of the New York State

      24      Trial Lawyers Association.

      25             I appear here today on behalf of the NYSTLA





 

                                                                   24
       1      board of directors, and our, roughly,

       2      3,500 attorney members who practice in trial, and

       3      appellate courts, throughout the state.

       4             I do thank the Committee, and

       5      Chairman Bonacic, for inviting us to participate

       6      today, and for the opportunity to speak in support

      10             I take the approach today from a personal

      11      standpoint than from the standpoint of the New York

      12      State Trial Lawyers' approach to the evaluation

      13      process, and based on my own personal interactions

      14      with Justice Abdus-Salaam at the trial-court level.

      15             For 60 years, NYSTLA has fought to protect

      16      equal access to the civil justice system for all

      17      New Yorkers.

      18             The constitutional right to a trial by jury

      19      is the foundation of that equal access, and NYSTLA

      20      vigorously opposes any compromise of this critical

      21      right, whether by legislation, or through the overly

      22      aggressive application of judicial doctrines and

      23      procedures, that can deny a worthy litigant their

      24      day in court.

      25             The appointment of a new judge to the





 

                                                                   25
       1      Court of Appeals is, therefore, always of great

       2      significance to the New York State Trial Lawyers

       3      Association.

       4             The legal rights of the hundreds of

       5      thousands of ordinary New Yorkers NYSTLA members

       6      represent depend on judicial restraint and careful

       7      application of the law by each member of the court.

       8             We applaud judges who demonstrate a

       9      preference for allowing cases to be presented to the

      10      jury, and who apply great caution in the use of

      11      summary judgment, and doctrines, such as

      12      collateral estoppel, that can sometimes prevent jury

      13      decisions from being made on the merits.

      16      New York State Commission on Judicial Nomination, to

      17      fill the vacancy created by the passing of

      18      Associate Judge Theodore T. Jones.

      19             Among such an impressively credentialed

      20      panel of candidates, Justice Abdus-Salaam stood out,

      21      both, for her judicial experience, as well as for

      22      her demonstrated commitment to a just and accessible

      23      legal system for all New Yorkers.

      24             Justice Abdus-Salaam is a calm, careful, and

      25      scholarly jurist, whose reputation for fairness





 

                                                                   26

       2             The committee rated Justice Abdus-Salaam as

       4             She is widely respected for her two decades

      10             Many NYSTLA members have had the honor of
